Patient note:
A 38-year-old woman employed as a software project manager arrived to the peri-operative medicine clinic this morning at the request of orthopedic surgery for a comprehensive review of her chronic medical conditions before scheduling arthroscopic repair of a recurrent right rotator-cuff tear sustained during recreational rock climbing; she walked briskly from the waiting room unaided and conversed comfortably throughout the visit. She was diagnosed at age 26 with systemic lupus erythematosus after episodes of photosensitive malar rash, symmetric morning stiffness of the metacarpophalangeal joints, intermittent low-grade fevers, and serologies notable for a strongly positive antinuclear antibody in a homogeneous pattern accompanied by anti-double-stranded DNA titers; since then she has been maintained on hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily and intermittent low-dose prednisone bursts for flares, with excellent adherence and no significant disease activity over the past two years. She has never experienced serositis, nephritis, central nervous system manifestations, or vasculitic skin ulcers, and her most recent urine study last month showed no protein, red blood cell casts, or cellular debris. A fasting comprehensive metabolic panel performed at that same visit revealed alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 62 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.0; liver ultrasound demonstrated mild hepatic steatosis without nodularity, normal portal and hepatic venous waveforms, and a spleen measuring 11 cm, findings her hepatologist attributes to long-standing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in the context of prior corticosteroid exposure. She denies pruritus, jaundice, abdominal distention, easy bruising, encephalopathy, hematemesis, melena, dyspepsia, or prior upper gastrointestinal ulcerations, and she has never required paracentesis, variceal banding, or diuretic therapy. Cardiovascular review is reassuring: she runs three kilometers on a treadmill three times weekly without chest pressure, radiating pain, diaphoresis, palpitations, dyspnea beyond expected exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or lower-extremity edema; she has never sustained a heart attack, been diagnosed with heart failure, or undergone valve surgery; an echocardiogram obtained one year ago as part of her autoimmune follow-up showed normal chamber dimensions, trivial tricuspid regurgitation, and a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 65 % with no regional wall-motion abnormalities. She has never undergone coronary angiography, stress testing, or cardiac hospitalization, and serial electrocardiograms remain in normal sinus rhythm without pathologic Q waves or repolarization changes. She has never been admitted for pneumonia, bronchospasm, or respiratory failure, does not carry inhalers, and climbs two flights of office stairs while carrying a backpack without wheeze or prolonged recovery. Neurologically she reports no transient unilateral weakness, facial droop, aphasia, diplopia, vision loss, seizures, or sudden sensory changes; she has never suffered a stroke or transient ischemic attack, and cranial magnetic resonance imaging obtained three years ago to evaluate migraine-like headaches was unremarkable, and today she demonstrates fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II through XII, 5/5 strength throughout, normal coordination, a steady tandem gait, and preserved recent and remote memory without any signs of cognitive decline. She does not experience calf claudication, rest pain, color change of the toes, or cold-induced digits, and distal pulses are readily palpable. Endocrine review notes that a workplace wellness screen two years prior revealed a fasting plasma glucose of 104 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c of 5.7 %; she adopted a lower-carbohydrate Mediterranean diet and increased aerobic exercise, and repeat testing last week showed fasting glucose 96 mg/dL and A1c 5.5 %, so no pharmacotherapy has been initiated. Renal function today is sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 105 mL/min/1.73 m²; urine microalbumin is <10 mg/g. There is no personal history of malignancy, lymphoma, or other hematologic disorders; her most recent Papanicolaou test and high-risk human papillomavirus co-testing last year were negative, a screening colonoscopy has not yet been indicated by age, and dermatologic surveillance shows only benign nevi. She tested negative for human immunodeficiency virus on two occasions while donating blood, her vaccination record is current for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, tetanus, and yearly influenza, and she received the two-dose recombinant zoster series last season. She drinks one glass of red wine on special occasions, denies past or present tobacco or illicit substance use, and has no known drug allergies. Family history reveals a mother with hypothyroidism and a father with hypertension diagnosed in his forties; there are no early myocardial infarctions, cerebrovascular accidents, connective-tissue disorders, or cirrhotic complications among first-degree relatives. Current medications are hydroxychloroquine as noted, prednisone 5 mg daily which she plans to taper under rheumatology guidance before surgery, calcium 600 mg with vitamin D3 800 IU twice daily, and a daily prenatal-formulation multivitamin; she stopped non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs two weeks ago on anesthesiology advice and uses acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed for shoulder pain. Vital signs in clinic: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 112/68 mm Hg seated in the right arm, pulse 72 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air, and body-mass index 23 kg/m². She appears well nourished, skin exam reveals faint healed malar erythema without active lesions, pharynx is clear, neck is supple with no cervical lymphadenopathy, jugular venous pulsation is less than 3 cm above the sternal angle, the cardiac point of maximal impulse is in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line and nondisplaced, S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, lungs are clear to auscultation with full aeration, abdomen is soft and nontender with a smooth liver edge palpated 1 cm below the right costal margin, and there is no splenomegaly or shifting dullness. Musculoskeletal examination shows tenderness over the supraspinatus insertion with painful arc from 70 to 110 degrees and preserved passive range of motion; small-joint inspection demonstrates no active synovitis or deformity. Distal pulses are 2+ and symmetric, capillary refill is <2 seconds, and no edema is present. The neurologic screen is unremarkable as described above. She requests confirmation that her autoimmune condition and mild hepatic enzyme elevation pose no contraindications to general anesthesia, seeks guidance on peri-operative steroid management, and wishes to understand whether any additional cardiac or pulmonary testing is warranted before proceeding with the planned outpatient procedure.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index sums weights for qualifying chronic diseases, with age points beginning at age 50 in the age-adjusted version.
- Age 38: 0 points.
- Connective tissue disease: established systemic lupus erythematosus qualifies even though it is currently quiet (1 point).
- Mild chronic liver disease: diagnosed non-alcoholic fatty liver disease with preserved synthetic function and no portal hypertension (1 point).
- Diabetes: prior borderline glycemia does not establish diabetes (0 points).
- No qualifying cardiac, vascular, cerebrovascular, pulmonary, renal, neurologic, ulcer, malignant, or AIDS diagnosis (0 additional points).
Total = 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
